story_title: The Mitten with the Small Stars

teller.name: Oriel Penhallow
teller.who: keeper of the Salt Lamp lighthouse at the north point

listener: a visitor sheltering from the wind in the lighthouse kitchen, by the stove
summary: Every autumn someone leaves mittens on the ferry wheel for Barnaby Teague, and tonight the secret knitter, Ines Larkspur, finishes this year's pair by the coal stove of the closed Green Kettle. She knits bands of stars and pine sprigs from an old Baltic pattern card and dozes with the pair on her knee.
source_tradition: Baltic folk knitting (patterned mittens with star and pine bands), Latvia and neighbouring coast
source_note: Traditional hand-knitting patterns are a folk craft in the public domain; the story, characters and wording are entirely original.

description_summary: Every autumn a pair of mittens appears on the Fernwick ferry wheel with no note; tonight the lighthouse keeper tells who leaves them, while a coal stove burns low.
description_setting: Mid October in Fernwick. The Green Kettle tea room has closed for the night, the coal stove is low and warm, and Ines Larkspur knits a star and pine mitten from an old Baltic pattern card while Pip the cat sleeps on the tiles.
image_brief: Inside a small seaside tea room at night: a worn armchair beside a squat black coal stove glowing orange through its little iron door, a willow knitting basket with gray and cream wool and a star-patterned mitten resting on the chair, a cat curled asleep on the warm hearth tiles, six cups in a row on a wooden shelf, a fogged window showing harbor lamps outside.
short_excerpt: Every autumn, on the first truly cold morning, Barnaby Teague finds a pair of mittens waiting for him on the wheel of the Wren Island ferry. They come wrapped in brown paper and tied with a length of red wool. There is never a note. Barnaby has piloted that ferry for twenty-two years, and in all that time he has never found out who leaves them. I know who it is. I have known for years. And since the lamp up here turns all night whether I watch it or not, I will tell you.
new_world_facts: Ines has secretly left a pair of mittens on Barnaby's ferry wheel every autumn for twenty-two years, wrapped in brown paper and tied with red wool, never with a note.
It began on the Green Kettle's first night, when Barnaby came in off a late ferry with hands too cold to hold a cup and warmed them on the teapot.
Barnaby believes Oriel Penhallow knits the mittens; Oriel cannot knit and has never corrected him.
This year's star and pine pattern card came from a biscuit tin bought at the Harvest Fair; on the back: stars to find the way home, pine to keep hands warm.
The six cups at the Green Kettle: blue, white, white, green, white, and one with a chipped gold rim.
Ines dries orange peel on top of the stove.
script:
[[CHAPTER Welcome]]

Welcome to Fernwick Nights. Tonight's story is The Mitten with the Small Stars, told by Oriel Penhallow, who keeps the lighthouse at the north point of Fernwick. Get comfortable, pull the blanket up a little higher, and let the evening slow down.

[long pause]

[[CHAPTER The Ferry Wheel]]

Come in out of the wind and sit by the stove. The kettle has only just boiled. There. Now, every autumn, on the first truly cold morning, Barnaby Teague finds a pair of mittens waiting for him on the wheel of the Wren Island ferry. They come wrapped in brown paper and tied with a length of red wool. There is never a note. Barnaby has piloted that ferry for twenty-two years, and in all that time he has never found out who leaves them. I know who it is. I have known for years. And since the lamp up here turns all night whether I watch it or not, I will tell you.

[pause]

Fernwick is a small town on a quiet stretch of coast. There is a harbor with a dozen fishing boats, this lighthouse at the north point, and one cobbled lane of shops along the water, called Harbor Lane. It is the middle of October. The leaves on the green have gone the color of toast, the evenings smell of chimney smoke and wet stone, and the first cold morning cannot be very far away. Down at the far end of Harbor Lane is a tea room called the Green Kettle, and in it, tonight, one mitten is still waiting to be finished.

[pause]

[[CHAPTER The Green Kettle]]

The woman who keeps the Green Kettle is Ines Larkspur. By this hour the last customer has gone, the sign in the door has been turned to Closed, and the six tables have been wiped until the old wood shines. Ines carries the cups to the shelf behind the counter and sets them in a row: blue, white, white, green, white, and the one with the chipped gold rim. She moves the green cup to the front, studies it, and puts it back exactly where it was. She does this every evening. Every evening the cups end up just as they started, and every evening she is satisfied. I have watched her do it a hundred times, and I still do not know what she is checking for.

[pause]

Then she sees to the stove. It is a squat black coal stove with a little iron door and a chimney pipe that disappears into the ceiling. When she opens the door, a wave of heat touches her face, and the smell of hot iron and coal dust drifts into the room. Inside, the fire has burned down to a bed of orange, with a thin blue flame walking slowly along the top. She tips three lumps from the scuttle, closes the door with the toe of her shoe, and listens. The stove ticks twice, the way it always does, and settles into a low, contented mutter.

[pause]

The window beside the stove has fogged at the corners. Through the clear middle of the glass, Harbor Lane is empty and shining from an afternoon shower. The street lamps along the water make small yellow pools on the cobbles, and the masts of the fishing boats rock very slightly against a sky the color of plums. Inside, the room is the warmest it has been all day. It smells of toast crusts and black tea, and faintly of the orange peel Ines dries on top of the stove, curling slowly into little brown spirals.

[long pause]

So she fetches her knitting basket from beneath the counter. It is an old willow basket with a lid that has never quite shut, and it creaks when she lifts it. Inside are two balls of wool, one the gray of wet slate and one the cream of fresh milk, and a set of five thin steel needles, cool to the touch. A finished mitten lies folded at the bottom. Its partner hangs from the needles, done as far as the thumb.

[pause]

[[CHAPTER How It Began]]

The mittens began twenty-two winters ago, on the night Ines first opened the Green Kettle. A strong wind had kept the ferry out late, and when it finally came in, a tall, quiet man in a salt-stiff coat walked through her door and asked for tea. His hands were so cold he could not hold the cup. He wrapped them around the warm teapot instead and stood like that, saying nothing, until the color came back into his knuckles. Ines poured him a second cup and did not charge him for either. The next autumn, she knitted her first pair.

[pause]

She never told him. Barnaby is a man who would thank someone so many times that they would both have to move to another town, and Ines did not want to move. So the mittens arrive on the ferry wheel in brown paper, and Barnaby wears them every day until spring. He also has a theory, which he once shared with the whole tea room, that I knit them, up here in the lamp room on the long nights. I cannot knit a single stitch. I have never corrected him, and neither has Ines. Some things are nicer left a little bit unexplained.

[pause]

How do I know? From up here, a keeper sees the whole harbor. One cold morning, years ago, just before the sun came up, I saw a small figure in a long green coat walk down to the ferry with a brown paper parcel under her arm. She tied it to the wheel, looked once along the empty quay, and walked home again with her hands in her pockets. The next time I took tea at the Green Kettle, Ines poured mine without a word and gave me the cup with the chipped gold rim. That was all either of us ever said about it.

[pause]

Ines settles into the chair beside the stove, the one with the cushion that has long ago taken her shape. The chair gives a small creak of welcome. She props her feet on the low stool, balances a cup of tea on the wide wooden arm, though the tea went lukewarm an hour ago, and lifts the needles into the warm light.

[pause]

[[CHAPTER Stars and Pine]]

This year's pattern came from a biscuit tin she found at the Harvest Fair. Under the paper lining was a pattern card, folded in four and worn soft as cloth. On it, in faded squares of pencil, was a band of tiny stars, then a band of pine sprigs, then stars again. On the back, someone had written two lines in a small, slanting hand. Stars, so the wearer can find the way home in the dark. Pine, so the hands stay warm the way the pine stays green all winter.

[pause]

It is a very old kind of pattern. On the coast across the northern sea, where the winters are long and the nights are longer, people once knitted mittens by the dozen. A young woman might fill a whole wooden chest with them before she married, each pair worked in a different pattern, and give them away to the people she loved. Every star and every little tree on them meant something. Ines likes that. She likes the idea of a wish that can be worn on a cold hand.

[long pause]

She knits one row of cream, then one row of gray. The wool runs over her finger and under, over and under, and the two colors twist together at the back, where no one will ever see them. The steel needles click softly, warm now from her hands. The stove ticks. After a while the clicking and the ticking fall into the same slow time, like two clocks in one room that have quietly agreed on the hour.

[pause]

Just above the thumb, the first star appears. It is a small cream diamond on a gray field, no bigger than a lentil. Ines turns the mitten toward the stove light to look at it and nods. Then she begins the second star beside it, and the third, until a little row of them runs across the back of the hand, like the lamps along Harbor Lane seen from the deck of a ferry coming home.

[pause]

Somewhere in the middle of the stars, she starts to hum. It is no particular tune, just a few low notes that wander up and down and end up where they began. She has hummed it for so many winters that she no longer notices she is doing it. The stove seems to like it. On each long note, the coal behind the little iron door glows a shade brighter.

[pause]

Pip comes in from the back room. Nobody in Fernwick has ever been sure whose cat Pip is, but tonight Pip belongs to the Green Kettle. The cat crosses the floor without any hurry at all, sniffs the warm tiles in front of the stove, turns around twice, and lowers herself onto them in a slow, round heap. One ear swivels toward the clicking needles. Then it swivels back.

[pause]

The stars are done, and now the pine sprigs begin. Each sprig is a little feather of stitches, leaning to the left, gray on cream, and each one takes exactly nine rows. Ines counts them silently, without moving her lips. A lump of coal shifts and settles in the stove, and a few orange sparks drift up behind the glass and fade. She does not look up. Her hands know the way.

[pause]

On the shelf behind her, the six cups catch the stove light, each one holding a small orange glow in its curve. A teaspoon rests in the saucer of the green cup, where it has rested since closing. Outside, the lamplighter's bicycle ticks past the window and fades down the lane toward the harbor. The clock over the counter has been saying quarter to nine for some time now. It is a very patient clock.

[long pause]

[[CHAPTER A Pair]]

Ines reaches the top of the hand. She counts the stitches and finds the number she wanted. Now she begins to narrow the top, two stitches together at each side, so the mitten will close over the fingers like a small round roof. The rows grow shorter, and they go more quickly, and the last band of stars sits neatly across the knuckles.

[long pause]

Her eyes are heavy, and she lets them be. The needles go on for a few more rows, slower now. Over, under. Over, under. The wool is warm in her hands. The cream is almost the color of the stove light, and the gray is almost the color of the shadows in the corners, and together they look very much like the evening.

[pause]

The last row is done. She draws the wool through the final loops and pulls it gently snug. She holds the mitten up beside its partner. Two rows of stars across the back. Two bands of pine. Two small round roofs. A pair.

[long pause]

Tomorrow she will wrap them in brown paper and tie them with red wool, and before the sun is up she will walk down to the harbor and leave them on the ferry wheel. And I will be up here, watching the lamp, and I will see her go. But that is tomorrow. Tonight, the chair is warm, and the stove is low, and there is no hurry in the room at all.

[long pause]

She lays the mittens on her knee, stars facing up. Her hand rests on the soft wool. The tea sits cold on the arm of the chair. Pip stretches one paw toward the stove and sighs. The coal settles.

[long pause]

Along Harbor Lane, the lamps burn on, one after another, all the way down to the water. The ferry rocks at its mooring. The clock says quarter to nine.

[long pause]

[[SECOND]]

[[CHAPTER Once More, Slowly]]

Every autumn, someone leaves mittens on the ferry wheel for Barnaby. He has never known who.

[pause]

It is Ines. She sits by the stove in the Green Kettle, with the door locked and the lamps low.

[pause]

She knits gray and cream. Over, under. Over, under. The needles click. The stove ticks.

[long pause]

A row of small stars. Stars to find the way home. A band of pine. Pine to keep the hands warm.

[pause]

Pip sleeps on the warm tiles. The coal settles. The clock says quarter to nine.

[long pause]

The last row is done. A pair. Ines lays them on her knee.

[long pause]

Her hand rests on the wool. Her eyes close. The stove is low.

[long pause]

And that is the story of the mittens. The lamp is turning, the kettle is still warm, and you can stay here by the stove as long as you like.

[long pause]

Good night.
hook: Every autumn, someone leaves a pair of mittens on the ferry wheel for Barnaby Teague, and in twenty-two years he has never found out who.
context: Ines Larkspur, who runs the Green Kettle tea room on Harbor Lane, has secretly knitted Barnaby's mittens every year since the cold night he first came in from the ferry; tonight she finishes this year's pair, in an old Baltic pattern of stars and pine.
